meta.title: RevOps Health Scorecard
meta.subtitle: A 5-minute diagnostic for B2B SaaS operations

tiers.label: Critical
tiers.framing: You scored in the bottom quartile of B2B SaaS ops teams we've benchmarked. The good news: every pillar in this tier has a defined fix that pays back within 90 days.

tiers.label: At risk
tiers.framing: You scored in the lower-middle range — better than 30 to 40 percent of B2B SaaS teams. The gaps are specific and fixable. Companies that act on a scorecard like this typically move up one tier within 6 months.

tiers.label: Functional
tiers.framing: You scored in the upper-middle range — better than 60 to 70 percent of B2B SaaS teams. You're past the rough edges. The work now is compounding the gains in 2 to 3 specific pillars.

tiers.label: Mature
tiers.framing: You scored in the top quintile of B2B SaaS ops teams. Your work now is optimisation and scale, not foundation. The recommendations focus on what separates top quintile from top decile.

context.label: What stage is your company at?
What's your annual recurring revenue band?

pillars.name: Churn signal visibility
pillars.description: Whether you can see churn coming 60 to 90 days before it happens. Of all six pillars, this is the one with the clearest revenue impact. B2B SaaS median gross revenue retention sits at around 90 to 92 percent (SaaS Capital, 2026; Benchmarkit, 2025) — meaning 8 to 10 percent of customers leave every year. Top quartile companies reach 95 percent or higher. The difference is almost entirely about visibility.

questions.text: How far in advance can you reliably identify which customers are likely to churn?

options.label: We don't predict it — we find out at renewal time or when they tell us
We sometimes notice 30 days out, when usage drops or tickets spike
We have signals 60 to 90 days out for most accounts
We have a defined health score updated weekly, with 90+ day visibility

questions.text: Which of these churn signals do you actively track and review?

options.label: Login frequency or product usage drop
Support ticket volume or sentiment change
Engagement with QBRs or scheduled check-ins

questions.text: When an account shows churn risk, what happens next?

options.label: Nothing formal — CSMs handle it ad hoc
A CSM does a check-in call
We have a defined save play with steps and a stakeholder map
Save play is automated to trigger, tracked through to outcome

critical.title: Build the first version of an account health score this quarter
critical.body: You're operating without visibility into who's at risk, which means you're losing accounts you could have saved. Start simple: pick three signals (usage trend, support ticket count, time since last QBR) and score each account weekly. Even a basic 3-signal score, reviewed in a Monday CS standup, will surface 60 to 80 percent of preventable churn 30+ days earlier than you see it now.
critical.firstStep: Export your top 50 accounts and rate each one Red, Yellow, or Green based on those three signals. Schedule a 30-minute review with the CS team Friday.

impact.text: Recovering 2 to 3 accounts per quarter from preventable churn typically equals $50K to $150K in protected ARR for a $5M to $20M ARR company.
impact.scaledLine: At your scale ({band}), catching preventable churn early protects real revenue — lifting GRR even 5 points recovers {recovery} in ARR per year, since retained revenue is a direct percentage of your base.

at_risk.title: Move from anecdotal signals to a defined health score with weekly review
at_risk.body: You're seeing some signals but not catching them consistently. The next step is formalising what 'at risk' means — write down the score thresholds, who owns intervention at each tier, and what the playbook is. The discipline of weekly review is what separates teams that protect ARR from teams that hope.
at_risk.firstStep: Document your current implicit health-scoring rules. Then formalise them with explicit weights. Pilot for 30 days, refine based on what flagged correctly versus what missed.

impact.text: Companies moving from ad hoc to systematised health scoring typically lift GRR by 2 to 4 percentage points within 6 months.
impact.scaledLine: At your scale ({band}), moving from ad hoc to systematised health scoring typically lifts GRR 2 to 4 points within 6 months — worth {recovery} in protected ARR at the upper end of that range.

functional.title: Add leading indicators beyond usage
functional.body: You have the basics. The next layer is what most teams miss: stakeholder change tracking (champion leaving is a top churn predictor in B2B SaaS), engagement with QBRs, and contract complexity signals. Adding two more leading indicators to your health score typically lifts predictive accuracy by 15 to 25 percent.
functional.firstStep: For your bottom 10 health-scored accounts, dig into the qualitative signals you're not currently tracking. Identify which 1 or 2 you should formalise.

impact.text: Improved early detection typically protects an additional 1 to 2 percentage points of GRR.
impact.scaledLine: At your scale ({band}), the added early detection typically protects another 1 to 2 points of GRR — and since each point is roughly 1% of ARR, that compounds into real money at {recovery} for a 5-point swing.

mature.title: Productise your save plays and measure save rate as a metric
mature.body: At your maturity level, the work is to treat save plays as a product — versioned, A/B tested, optimised. Track save rate by play, by segment, by CSM. The teams in the top decile of GRR (97 percent or higher) treat their save motion the same way sales treats their deal motion.
mature.firstStep: Pick your two most-used save plays. Define what 'success' looks like for each. Start tracking save rate by play next month.

impact.text: Top-decile GRR companies see 1 to 3 additional NRR points compared to top quartile.
impact.scaledLine: At your scale ({band}), closing the gap from top quartile to top decile is worth 1 to 3 additional retention points — at this revenue level, even small retention gains translate to a band of {recovery} per 5-point move.

pillars.name: SLA and ops discipline
pillars.description: Whether your response and resolution times are measured and enforced. SLAs are the floor of operational trust. When customers know issues get handled, they extend grace during the inevitable hard moments. When they don't, every incident becomes a credibility test.

questions.text: What percentage of customer issues are resolved within your stated SLA?

options.label: We have SLAs but don't actively measure compliance
95 percent or higher compliance, measured weekly with breach RCAs

questions.text: When an issue gets escalated, the path is...

options.label: Escalates to a team lead, ad hoc
Documented escalation matrix with response time targets per severity
Documented escalation, automated routing, post-incident review for sev-1s

questions.text: How quickly can your team produce a customer-facing status update during an incident?

options.label: We figure it out during the incident
Under 30 minutes with templates and automated stakeholder notification

critical.title: Ship a one-page SLA document this month
critical.body: You have no measured response or resolution targets, which means there's nothing to enforce. Start with three tiers (Sev-1: 30-minute response and 4-hour resolution; Sev-2: 2-hour and 1-business-day; Sev-3: 1-business-day and 5-business-day). Publish it. Track compliance weekly. The act of measuring will improve compliance by 20 to 30 percent before you change anything else.
critical.firstStep: Pull your last 30 customer issues. Categorise them retroactively and measure response times. The gap between current performance and the SLA you'd want to publish is your starting baseline.

impact.text: Teams with measured SLAs see 30 to 50 percent fewer escalations to leadership over 6 months.

at_risk.title: Add severity-based escalation routing
at_risk.body: SLAs without an escalation matrix mean every breach becomes a fire. The next layer is documenting who gets paged for what — by issue severity, by hour of day, by customer tier. A one-page escalation matrix on the team wiki, reviewed quarterly, beats a Confluence labyrinth nobody reads.
at_risk.firstStep: Draft a 3-tier severity matrix with response time targets. Assign a primary and backup owner for each tier. Share with the team this Friday.

impact.text: Reduces incident-to-resolution time by 20 to 30 percent within the first quarter.

functional.title: Automate the SLA timer and breach alerts
functional.body: You're measuring. The next step is removing human latency from the measurement itself. Most ticket systems can fire a webhook 75 percent of the way through SLA — connect that to a Slack alert with the ticket owner and one fallback. Breach rates typically drop 40 to 60 percent the first month after this is wired up.
functional.firstStep: In your ticketing tool, set up 'approaching SLA' alerts at 75 percent time-elapsed for sev-1 and sev-2. Route to a channel with the assigned owner and their backup.

impact.text: 40 to 60 percent fewer SLA breaches within 30 days.

mature.title: Run quarterly SLA reviews with customers
mature.body: You're at a level where the next gain is making your operational rigour visible to the customer. Share your SLA performance in QBRs. Companies that show their compliance numbers to customers see measurably higher renewal rates because they've turned ops discipline into a trust signal.
mature.firstStep: Pick your top 5 accounts. Add a 1-slide SLA performance summary to their next QBR. Measure renewal sentiment versus accounts without it.

impact.text: Top-decile companies report 2 to 4 percentage point lifts in renewal rates from this practice.

pillars.name: Process documentation
pillars.description: Whether your most senior ops people could leave tomorrow without taking critical knowledge with them. Documentation is what separates orgs that compound knowledge from orgs that lose it every time someone leaves.

questions.text: If your most senior ops person left tomorrow, how much of their work could a replacement run from documentation alone?

options.label: Less than 25 percent — a lot lives in their head
25 to 50 percent — basics documented, edge cases aren't
50 to 75 percent — most of it, but some tribal knowledge remains
75 percent or more — documentation-first culture, runbooks for everything

questions.text: Which of these have current, used SOPs?

options.label: Internal handoffs (sales to CS, CS to support)

questions.text: How often are your SOPs reviewed and updated?

options.label: After every major incident, plus scheduled quarterly review

critical.title: Pick the one process that breaks most often. Document it this week.
critical.body: Trying to document everything at once is the failure mode. Start with the workflow that causes the most fire-drills — usually order-to-cash or escalation handling — and write a SIPOC-mapped SOP. One process, one week, then move to the next. After 8 weeks you have your eight most painful processes covered. That's 80 percent of operational risk.
critical.firstStep: Identify the process that's caused the most rework or escalation in the last 30 days. Block 90 minutes Friday to write its SOP. Use a SIPOC table at the top, then step-by-step procedure with decision points, then escalation matrix.

impact.text: Teams that document their top 5 processes see 40 to 60 percent fewer 'how do I' escalations to senior staff within a quarter.

critical.timeToImplement: 1 process per week, 8 weeks total for top processes

at_risk.title: Move from 'documentation exists' to 'documentation is used'
at_risk.body: Most ops teams have SOPs that nobody opens. The fix isn't more docs — it's putting them where work happens. Link the relevant SOP from the ticket type. Embed it in the onboarding checklist. Reference it by URL in Slack when someone asks. Documentation that gets opened gets updated; documentation that doesn't, decays.
at_risk.firstStep: Pick your 3 most-used SOPs. Find every place a new team member would look for that information. Add the link there.

impact.text: Documentation usage typically increases 3 to 5x with this single change.

functional.title: Add named SOP owners and a quarterly review cadence
functional.body: SOPs without owners decay silently. Assign each major SOP to one person, with calendar invites for quarterly review. The act of opening it for review forces the small fixes that prevent the big drift.
functional.firstStep: List your top 10 SOPs. Assign each one an owner. Send calendar invites for quarterly review (90, 180, 270, 360 days out).

impact.text: Documentation accuracy stays above 90 percent versus the typical 40 to 60 percent decay over 12 months.

mature.title: Convert your top 3 SOPs into automation specs
mature.body: When documentation is mature, the highest-value next step is using it as a blueprint for automation. Any SOP that's been stable for two quarters and runs more than 10 times per week is an automation candidate. Your SOPs are the spec; the automation is the implementation.
mature.firstStep: Identify your 3 most-run SOPs that have been stable for 6+ months. For each, sketch what 'fully automated' would look like.

impact.text: Each automated SOP typically saves 5 to 15 hours per week.

pillars.name: Automation maturity
pillars.description: How much manual work could be automated but isn't. Across B2B SaaS, revenue per employee has been rising as automation absorbs repetitive operational work (industry benchmarks, 2026). Manual work isn't free; it costs payroll plus error rate plus the opportunity cost of what those people could be doing instead.

questions.text: Estimate the hours per week your ops team spends on tasks that could be automated but aren't.
Which of these are automated end-to-end (no manual steps)?
When a new tool is added to your stack, how quickly does it integrate with existing systems?

options.label: It doesn't really integrate — tools live in silos
Manual exports and imports between systems
API integrations done case-by-case, takes weeks
Integration is part of tool adoption — connected within days

critical.title: Pick the single most repetitive manual workflow and automate it this month
critical.body: You're losing 30+ hours per week to manual work that compounds into real money. The fastest win is usually order validation, lead routing, or renewal alerts — workflows where the rules are clear and the volume is high. Use n8n, Make, or Zapier for the first build; you don't need custom code for 80 percent of automation work.
critical.firstStep: List the top 5 most-repeated manual tasks the team did last week. Pick the one with clearest rules. Build it in n8n in a single afternoon.

impact.text: The first automation typically returns 3 to 5 hours per week. After 6 automations, teams report 20 to 30 percent capacity recovery.

at_risk.title: Build an 'automation backlog' and ship one per week
at_risk.body: Teams plateau at this tier because they automate sporadically. The fix is treating automation as an ongoing function: maintain a backlog, prioritise by hours-saved-per-week, ship one new automation each week. Eight weeks of this and you're in the top quartile of operational efficiency.
at_risk.firstStep: Create a simple Notion or Airtable backlog. Add every manual task you notice this week with an estimated hours-saved-per-week.

impact.text: 20 to 40 percent of team capacity typically recovered within 2 quarters.

functional.title: Move from automation to orchestration
functional.body: You've automated individual workflows. The next layer is connecting them — when a renewal alert fires, it should trigger the QBR scheduling, pull the latest health score, and prep the renewal play in one motion. Tools like n8n and Make support this; most teams just don't think to wire it up.
functional.firstStep: Pick your two most-related automations. Sketch how they could trigger each other. Build the connection this week.

impact.text: Orchestrated workflows typically cut total cycle time by 40 to 60 percent over individual automations.

mature.title: Add LLM-powered judgment to your automation layer
mature.body: You've automated the deterministic work. The frontier now is automating the parts that previously required human judgment — categorising tickets by intent, drafting first-pass responses, summarising QBR calls into action items. Claude or GPT in your n8n flows can save another 10 to 20 hours per week beyond what rules-based automation reaches.
mature.firstStep: Pick one workflow that currently requires human judgment but follows a pattern. Add an LLM step. Test for 30 days against human output.

impact.text: 10 to 20 additional hours per week recovered, on top of rules-based automation.

pillars.name: Data and reporting
pillars.description: Whether leadership can see what they need without asking. The cost of bad data isn't the wrong dashboard. It's the meeting that runs long because two people have different numbers. It's the decision delayed because someone has to double-check the source.

questions.text: When the CEO asks 'how are we doing on accounts this month', how long does it take to get an answer?

options.label: Hours to a day — someone has to pull and reconcile data
30 minutes — dashboard exists but needs interpretation
5 minutes — they pull it themselves from a dashboard
Real-time — there's a leadership dashboard always-on

questions.text: How confident are you that the numbers in your CRM and dashboards match reality?

options.label: Honestly, the data is messy — we don't fully trust it
Trust the headline metrics, distrust the breakdowns
High confidence — data hygiene is a tracked metric

questions.text: Your reporting cadence is best described as...

options.label: Weekly snapshot reports, mostly lagging metrics
Weekly plus monthly with leading indicators
Real-time dashboards plus scheduled deep-dives plus leading and lagging metrics

critical.title: Build one always-on leadership dashboard this month
critical.body: When the CEO has to ask, you've already lost. The fix is one dashboard, four KPIs, refreshed daily — ARR, GRR, account count by tier, active escalations. That's it. Don't try to solve all reporting at once. Looker Studio or Metabase can both do this in a day if you have the data.
critical.firstStep: Decide the four KPIs leadership cares about most. Connect them to whatever CRM you use. Share the dashboard URL in Slack daily for a week to build the habit of looking at it.

impact.text: Companies typically reclaim 4 to 8 hours per week of senior time previously spent answering ad-hoc data questions.

at_risk.title: Add data hygiene as a tracked metric
at_risk.body: Numbers you don't trust are worse than no numbers, because they cause overconfidence. Pick three data quality metrics — percentage of accounts with current owner, percentage of opportunities with close date, percentage of contacts with valid email — and track them monthly. Set targets. Assign an owner.
at_risk.firstStep: Run a one-time audit on those three metrics. Publish the baseline. Set a target 6 months out. Assign an owner.

impact.text: Data trust scores typically improve 30 to 50 percent within 2 quarters.

functional.title: Layer in leading indicators alongside lagging ones
functional.body: Most reporting at this tier is lagging — what happened last month. The next step is adding leading indicators that predict what's coming: pipeline coverage ratio, expansion signals, health score distribution, time-to-close trending. Leading indicators give the team 30 to 60 days of warning before lagging metrics shift.
functional.firstStep: Pick 2 leading indicators that map to your biggest revenue risks. Add them to the leadership dashboard alongside lagging metrics.

impact.text: Earlier course-correction typically protects 1 to 3 percentage points of ARR per year.

mature.title: Push self-service deeper into the org
mature.body: At your tier, the next gain is making non-ops people fluent in the data. Train CSMs to query their own account-level data. Train sales to pull their own pipeline reports. Every question a non-ops team can answer themselves is a question that doesn't interrupt the ops team.
mature.firstStep: Pick one team (CS or sales). Run a 1-hour training on the dashboard most relevant to them. Track their dashboard logins for a month.

impact.text: Ops team capacity typically increases 10 to 20 percent as ad-hoc query load drops.

pillars.name: Renewal and expansion
pillars.description: Whether you protect renewals 60+ days out and treat expansion as a tracked motion. In B2B SaaS, most net new ARR at scale now comes from existing customers rather than new logos — expansion is the dominant growth channel above roughly $50M ARR and a major one well below it (Optifai / ChartMogul, 2026).

questions.text: When does the renewal conversation typically start with a customer?

options.label: After the renewal date passes, or when the customer brings it up
120+ days out, with a defined renewal play

questions.text: For your top 20 percent of accounts, how clear is the expansion path?

options.label: We don't have an expansion strategy per account
We pitch expansion when usage indicates it
Each top account has documented expansion opportunities and a named owner
Expansion is forecast like new sales — pipeline, stages, win rates

questions.text: What's your gross revenue retention (GRR) over the last 12 months?

options.label: Don't track GRR, or below 80 percent

critical.title: Move every renewal conversation to 90 days out
critical.body: You're losing renewals you could have saved because you're starting the conversation too late. Block one hour every Monday to review every account renewing in the next 120 days. That single calendar habit — without changing anything else — will lift renewal rates 5 to 10 percentage points within two quarters.
critical.firstStep: Pull a list of every account renewing in the next 120 days. Assign each one to a CSM with a date for the first renewal touch. Track progress weekly.

impact.text: For a $5M ARR company at 85 percent GRR, lifting GRR to 90 percent recovers ~$250K of ARR per year.
impact.scaledLine: At your scale ({band}), starting renewals 90 days out instead of late typically lifts renewal rates 5 to 10 points — and since GRR gains are a direct percentage of ARR, a 5-point lift is worth {recovery} per year.

at_risk.title: Document expansion paths for your top 20 accounts
at_risk.body: Expansion that 'happens when CSMs have time' doesn't happen. The fix is making expansion a tracked motion: each top account gets an expansion hypothesis (what additional product, seats, or tier they could grow into), an owner, and a target close date. This single change typically lifts NRR by 4 to 6 percentage points within 6 months.
at_risk.firstStep: List your top 20 accounts. For each, write one sentence: 'This account could grow by [X] if we [Y].' Assign an owner.

impact.text: 4 to 6 NRR percentage points within 6 months for teams that adopt this.
impact.scaledLine: At your scale ({band}), making expansion a tracked motion typically lifts NRR 4 to 6 points within 6 months — at this revenue level, even a 5-point retention swing is worth {recovery} in ARR per year.

functional.title: Forecast expansion like a sales pipeline
functional.body: You have expansion paths. The next layer is treating expansion deals with the same rigour as new business — stages, win rates, weighted forecasts, weekly review. Most CS teams resist this because it feels like sales. The teams that adopt it consistently outperform those that don't, by 8 to 12 NRR points.
functional.firstStep: Build a simple pipeline view of your top 20 accounts' expansion opportunities. Include stage, value, expected close date. Review weekly with CS leadership.

impact.text: 8 to 12 NRR percentage points for teams that fully adopt this.
impact.scaledLine: At your scale ({band}), forecasting expansion like a sales pipeline typically lifts NRR 8 to 12 points — and at this revenue base, that range of retention improvement maps to {recovery} or more per year.

mature.title: Build a customer growth scorecard at the account level
mature.body: At your maturity, the next layer is account-level growth modeling: which accounts have the highest expansion potential, which CSMs convert that potential best, which products have the highest cross-sell rate. This is where NRR moves from 110 to 125 percent.
mature.firstStep: Pick 3 dimensions to track per account: expansion potential score, engagement depth, cross-sell readiness. Score every top-tier account next quarter.

impact.text: Top-decile NRR companies see this analytics layer compound into 5 to 10 additional NRR points over 18 months.
impact.scaledLine: At your scale ({band}), an account-level growth layer compounds into 5 to 10 additional NRR points over 18 months — at this revenue level, each 5-point increment is worth {recovery} per year.

below_80.opening: Your reported gross revenue retention sits below 80 percent, beneath the B2B SaaS floor — SaaS Capital's 2026 benchmark puts the private-company median at 91 percent.

clauses.supported: Your churn signal visibility and renewal motion both score well, which means the machinery to fix this is already in place; a number this low against strong operations usually points to a recent, specific shock — a segment churning, a pricing change, a single large loss — rather than a systemic gap.
clauses.churn_weak: Your churn signal visibility scores low, which means you cannot yet see the churn driving this number 60 to 90 days before it lands — so accounts are being lost that earlier visibility would have surfaced in time to save.
clauses.renewal_weak: Your renewal motion scores low, which means renewals and expansion are not yet run as a defended, proactive motion — so revenue you have already earned is leaking at the renewal point rather than being protected.
clauses.both_weak: Your churn signal visibility and renewal motion both score low, so the cause is structural rather than circumstantial: you cannot yet see churn coming, and there is no defended renewal motion to stop it once it starts.

below_80.closerSupported: Point the operational discipline you already have at the specific cohort dragging the number down, and it should recover quickly.
below_80.closerUnsupported: Until this is addressed, no growth investment will compound, because revenue leaks out the bottom faster than new bookings replace it — this is the first thing to fix, ahead of everything else.

80_90.opening: Your reported GRR of 80 to 90 percent sits just below the B2B SaaS median of 91 percent (SaaS Capital, 2026).

clauses.supported: Your churn signal visibility and renewal motion both score well, so the trajectory points up rather than down — the foundation to close the gap is already in place.
clauses.churn_weak: The constraint is churn signal visibility, which scores low: you cannot yet see the churn that erodes this number 60 to 90 days out, so the gap to the median persists because losses are caught too late to prevent.
clauses.renewal_weak: The constraint is your renewal motion, which scores low: renewals and expansion are not yet run as a proactive, defended motion, so revenue slips at the renewal point that a tighter motion would hold.
clauses.both_weak: With churn signal visibility and renewal motion both scoring low, this number rests on weak foundations and tends to slip rather than climb — neither early churn detection nor a proactive renewal motion is yet defending it.

80_90.closerSupported: Lifting GRR by five points typically recovers five to six percent of ARR, and with the foundation already built, that gain is a matter of consistent execution rather than new infrastructure.
80_90.closerUnsupported: The path to the 95 percent-plus top quartile starts with building that visibility and discipline now — lifting GRR by five points typically recovers five to six percent of ARR, which is the single highest-return move available at this level.

90_95.opening: Your reported GRR of 90 to 95 percent is at or above the B2B SaaS median of 91 percent (SaaS Capital, 2026).

clauses.supported: Your churn signal visibility and renewal motion both score well, so this retention is operationally earned rather than borrowed — the number reflects a system, not luck.
clauses.churn_weak: But read it with some caution: your churn signal visibility scores low, which means you cannot yet see the churn that would erode this number 60 to 90 days out, so the retention is less defended than the figure suggests.
clauses.renewal_weak: But read it with some caution: your renewal motion scores low, which means renewals and expansion are not yet run as a defended, proactive motion, so this number rests on weaker foundations than it appears.
clauses.both_weak: But read it with caution: your churn signal visibility and renewal motion both score low, which means this retention is not yet operationally defended — high GRR built on weak visibility tends to revert, because you are holding on through goodwill and inertia rather than a repeatable system.

90_95.closerSupported: The next leverage is the climb to the 95 percent-plus top quartile, which is less about preventing churn and more about systematic expansion — forecasting renewals like a pipeline and treating expansion as a tracked motion.
90_95.closerUnsupported: Build that operational defence now, while the number is still healthy, rather than after it slips — retention is far cheaper to protect than to rebuild.

95_plus.opening: Your reported GRR of 95 percent or higher would place you in the B2B SaaS top quartile (SaaS Capital, 2026).

clauses.supported: Your churn signal visibility and renewal motion both score well, so the number is operationally defended — this is the strongest position in the dataset, retention this high backed by the systems to hold it.
clauses.churn_weak: But your churn signal visibility scores low, an unusual pairing with retention this strong: you cannot yet see the churn that erodes the number 60 to 90 days before it lands, so it is held more by inertia than by a system that would catch a downturn early.
clauses.renewal_weak: But your renewal motion scores low, an unusual pairing with retention this strong: renewals and expansion are not yet run as a defended, proactive motion, so the number is more exposed than top-quartile retention should be.
clauses.both_weak: But your churn signal visibility and renewal motion both score low, an unusual and unstable combination: either the number reflects a young book that has not yet faced its first full renewal wave, or GRR is being measured generously.

95_plus.closerSupported: The frontier from here is net revenue retention — turning that retained base into systematic expansion, where the best B2B SaaS companies reach 118 percent and above (Optifai, 2026).
95_plus.closerUnsupported: Pressure-test how GRR is calculated, then build that operational defence now, while the number is healthy — top-quartile retention without the operations to support it rarely holds beyond a few quarters.
